meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Who decided Owen gets a zero, and did anyone hear him first?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.

Conclusive. Turnitin's own guide says its score shouldn't be the sole basis for punishing a student, and I have it printed in my bag. You still haven't told me who decided, or whether anyone heard Owen first.

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. What else do you have?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
11:31, 11:52, 11:58. I'm writing those down. He wrote it over the weekend, and people paste drafts in from somewhere else all the time.

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Turn it closer. A seventeen-year-old misremembering a line or citing the wrong scene is a careless mistake, not proof of anything.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Kids change their thesis between an outline and a final draft. That's what an outline is for.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

So he was heard for five minutes after class, with no parent there, and the only record of it is your own notes. Forty minutes under a clock in September is not a take-home essay. I want the version history and the September piece sent to me in writing.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

That's 4.4, and Owen does it to put this behind him, not because he did anything. Private, not in front of his class, and nothing on his record, in writing tonight. The zero comes out of the gradebook the day his rewrite is marked, Hale.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Thursday after school. Who supervises him in the room?
Do we have an agreement?
Yes, once you tell me who is in that room with him on Thursday.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed to a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes under procedure 4.4 this Thursday, November 12, after school, not in front of his class, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing placed on Owen's record. I still want to know who will supervise him in that room, and I want the version history and his September in-class piece sent to me in writing. I expect that agreement in writing tonight, as you promised.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: last position; she agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday with nothing on his record, and she still wants the agreement in writing tonight, the name of whoever supervises him, and the documents on paper; that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, reached before her time ran out.
What moved her: you turned the screen and walked her through the version history with its exact times, because it was dated, tied to Owen's own file, and something she could check herself.
What cost ground: you opened with the checker score and called it conclusive, which handed her the one argument she had come prepared to win.
What she never said: in October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history put the essay being written late at night the evening before it was due, very close to that kind of night; that proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: when she first sat down and asked who decided and whether Owen was heard, open by owning the zero and telling her about your November 2 conversation with him, and leave the checker score out entirely.
